Assurance of Faith
uh-SHOOR-ance of FAITH
n. phrase (Reformed soteriology; pastoral theology)
From Old French assurer (to secure, to make certain, from Latin ad- + securus, safe, secure) + Old English geleafa (faith, belief, from gelefan, to believe); in Reformed pastoral theology, the Spirit-wrought confidence that one is truly united to Christ and an heir of salvation.

See also: Assurance of Faith

Biblical Definition

Assurance of faith is the Spirit-wrought, Scripture-grounded confidence that a believer is truly united to Christ, genuinely regenerated, and a secure heir of eternal life. John writes his first epistle explicitly for this purpose: “These things I have written to you who believe in the name of the Son of God — so that you may know that you have eternal life” (1 Jn 5:13). The knowledge here is not mere intellectual acknowledgment but settled, Spirit-confirmed certainty. Paul exemplifies it in the face of suffering: “For this reason I also suffer these things — but I am not ashamed, for I know whom I have believed, and I am persuaded that He is able to guard what I have entrusted to Him until that Day” (2 Tim 1:12). The assurance is not self-generated confidence; it is the fruit of resting on the Word and promise of God. Hebrews calls the church to “draw near with a sincere heart, in full assurance of faith” (Heb 10:22), linking assurance directly to the completed priestly work of Christ and the sprinkled blood that speaks forgiveness. The definitive ground of assurance is the completed work of Christ and the promises of the covenant; the subjective means is the inner witness of the Holy Spirit: “The Spirit Himself testifies with our spirit that we are children of God” (Rom 8:16). The 1689 LBCF (18.1–4) treats assurance as “infallible certainty” that genuine believers may attain — not belonging to the essence of faith, but obtainable through the exercise of faith and obedience and the Spirit's inward testimony.

Webster 1828 Definition

The Spirit-wrought, Scripture-grounded confidence that a genuine believer is united to Christ and an heir of eternal life — not belonging to the bare essence of saving faith, but attainable by the exercise of faith and obedience and the inner witness of the Holy Spirit, as the 1689 LBCF (18.1–4) affirms.

ASSURANCE OF FAITH, n. phrase. The settled, Spirit-confirmed confidence that one is a genuine child of God — grounded in the promises of the covenant, the completed work of Christ, and the inward witness of the Holy Spirit.

The Reformed tradition carefully distinguishes assurance from the bare act of saving faith. Faith is the act of resting on Christ for salvation; assurance is the confidence that one has genuinely so rested and that the fruit of that resting is present. Faith without assurance is possible; assurance without faith is not.

The 1689 LBCF (18.2) identifies three grounds of assurance: (1) the divine truth of the promises of salvation in Scripture; (2) the inward evidence of the graces of the Spirit (1 John 2:3; 3:9–14); (3) the testimony of the Spirit of adoption, witnessing with the believer's spirit (Rom 8:15–16). These three working together produce the “infallible certainty” the Confession names.

The Roman Catholic position denied that a believer could have certainty of his own salvation apart from special revelation — treating such certainty as presumption (Council of Trent, Session 6). The Reformers rejected this as a corruption of the gospel: the certainty of salvation rests on Christ's sufficiency and the faithfulness of God, not on the believer's own moral performance, which is always incomplete.

Assurance may be shaken by sin, spiritual drought, and Satanic attack — the Psalms record many such seasons. But it is recoverable through renewed attention to the means of grace, the promises of the Word, and prayer for the Spirit's renewing testimony.

Key Scripture

1 John 5:13 — "These things I have written to you who believe in the name of the Son of God — so that you may know that you have eternal life."

2 Timothy 1:12 — "For this reason I also suffer these things — but I am not ashamed, for I know whom I have believed, and I am persuaded that He is able to guard what I have entrusted to Him until that Day."

Hebrews 10:22 — "let us draw near with a sincere heart, in full assurance of faith — having our hearts sprinkled clean from an evil conscience, and our bodies washed with pure water."

Romans 8:16 — "The Spirit Himself testifies with our spirit that we are children of God."

Modern Corruption

Rome denied that ordinary believers could have certainty of salvation, treating such assurance as presumption; antinomian “easy believism” treats profession of faith as automatically producing assurance without reference to the Spirit's inward witness or the fruit of regeneration.

expand to see more

The Council of Trent (1547) declared that no one can know with the certainty of faith that he has obtained God's grace, unless through special revelation — a position designed to keep believers dependent on the sacramental system for any hope of assurance. This is a pastoral corruption of the first order: it removes from the believer the comfort of the promises of God and substitutes the anxiety of ongoing performance. The Reformers' answer was to ground assurance in the completed work of Christ and the Spirit's testimony, not in the accumulation of sacramental participation. Certainty of salvation is not presumption; it is the privilege of every genuine believer who rests on the faithfulness of God.

The American evangelical corruption runs in the opposite direction: “easy believism” — the revivalist teaching that assurance of salvation is produced simply by a past prayer or decision — short-circuits the Spirit's threefold grounds and produces false assurance in the unregenerate. A person who prayed a prayer at age seven but shows no fruit of the Spirit, no love for the Word, no repentance, no growth in holiness, is given assurance by easy believism that the Scripture does not grant. The 1689 LBCF requires that assurance be supported by the inward evidence of the graces of the Spirit — not the remembrance of a past act.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Old French assurer (to make secure, certain) from Latin ad-securus (made safe, secured); in Reformed pastoral theology, assurance is the confident security of a believer in Christ, grounded in objective promises and confirmed by the Spirit's inward testimony.

expand to see more

Latin securus — safe, secure, free from care; the root conveys settled safety rather than anxious self-examination — the security God's promises produce.

Greek plêrophoria — full assurance, complete confidence (Heb 10:22; Col 2:2); the New Testament word for the fullness of settled certainty the Spirit produces.

Greek oida — I know with settled certainty (1 Jn 5:13: “so that you may know”); John uses the perfect tense of knowing, conveying settled, established knowledge rather than tentative opinion.

Latin testimonium Spiritus Sancti internum — the internal testimony of the Holy Spirit; Calvin's phrase for the Spirit's witness to Scripture and to the believer's adoption, the subjective ground of assurance.

Greek symmartyrei — testifies together with (Rom 8:16); the Spirit co-witnesses with the believer's own spirit — the assurance is not self-generated but a joint testimony of two witnesses.

Usage

"Assurance of faith is not the same as certainty about one's eternal destiny based on past profession; it is the living, Spirit-confirmed confidence of present union with Christ, confirmed by ongoing fruit."

"The believer who lacks assurance is called to examine himself (2 Cor 13:5), attend the means of grace, and pray for the Spirit's renewing testimony — not to manufacture assurance by force of will."

"A church that cultivates genuine assurance — grounded in Christ's sufficiency, confirmed by the Spirit's witness, and evidenced by grace-produced fruit — produces both humble confidence and holy living."
